_note: Answers written by the system that the editor holds after reading them (site/build.js never shows the version that is held; scripts/editor/release_auto.py does not let it out). Each with the day and the reason. 'lane' (18 November 2026, lane 19): the lane that wrote the version the editor read; a hold is of that version, so an answer written again by a newer lane is judged afresh by the gates and is not held by this entry. 'say': what the editor found, in a sentence for the writer; the lane gives it to the writer of the next version (scripts/auto/lane.py, held_say), so that a held answer is written again by itself. 'run' (18 November 2026, site 2.21.1): the hold is of the one version that run wrote (the record's made.run); the same lane's next version, written with what the editor found, is judged afresh and shown.

held.why: read by the editor on 17 November 2026 and not let out: its first sentence says 'It can make sex feel better', an effect, where both sources give what people who use cannabis report and what use is linked to (their own words are under the lines: 'has been associated with', 'see benefits'); its But is a remark on one study's measuring and says without a source that the amount changes the effect. The second sentence ('People who use cannabis report ...') is right. To be written again once a rule for this has been measured on the exams.
held.say: Both sources give what people who use cannabis REPORT, and what cannabis use is LINKED to. Do not say as a fact that cannabis makes sex better: say what people report, as a report (People who use cannabis report ...), or what use has been linked to. Let the But be a limit the sources state about those reports (who was asked, that they chose to answer), not a remark that the amount changes the effect.

held.why: read by the editor on 18 November 2026 (it waited because it disagreed with the checked claim cl_meth_dopamine_damage, and it does): its line on damage gives as a fact about amphetamines and methamphetamine what its source, a 2009 review, reports from laboratory animals given high doses (that review's own first words: 'clearly neurotoxic in laboratory animals'). The checked claim says lasting loss of dopamine nerve cells in people is not shown either way. Not let out; written again by itself.
held.say: The damage to nerve cells that the 2009 review describes is from laboratory animals given high doses. Say so in the sentence (in laboratory animals), or leave damage out. Never state it as a fact about people.

held.why: read by the editor on 18 November 2026 (it waited because it disagreed with the checked claim cl_mdma_neurotoxicity_contested, and it does): its short answer says 'MDMA damages serotonin nerves, while amphetamines damage serotonin and dopamine nerves' as a fact, where the source's findings are from laboratory animals and its own words are 'not yet proven' for humans. Not let out; written again by itself.
held.say: The review's findings on damage to nerves are from laboratory animals given high doses, and it says itself that this is not yet proven in humans. Do not put damage in the short answer as a fact; if a line names it, say in laboratory animals.

held.why: read by the editor on 18 November 2026 (it waited for a further reader that could not be asked): 'A 2020 analysis says it may help anxiety and depression' leaves out that the analysis was of psilocybin combined with psychotherapy, words that narrow what was found; and it writes 'cancer patients'. Not let out; written again by itself.
held.say: The official page says psilocybin COMBINED WITH PSYCHOTHERAPY: keep those words wherever you report that analysis. Write people with cancer, not cancer patients.

held.why: read by the editor on 18 November 2026 (it waited as an answer about children): it answers a question about adults with the half-lives measured in two young children after an accident, and says the drug 'stayed in the body for' the time in which half of it leaves. Not an answer to the question. Not let out; written again by itself.
held.say: The question is how long cannabis can be found in the body of a person who used it. A case report of two young children is not an answer to it, and a half-life is not how long a drug stays. Rest the short answer on a review or an official page.

held.why: read by the editor on 18 November 2026 (held for the editor's reading of answers about amounts): row 10 ('the dose regimen of 35-50 mg/70kg', from the summary of a 2026 meta-analysis) reads as an amount that an analysis worked out, not one that a study gave to people; row 9 names nobody ('Participants'). Not let out; the lane as it is now writes it again (its rules since lane 13 refuse an amount that was estimated or called optimal).

read by the editor on 18 November 2026 (held for the editor's reading of answers about amounts): row 1 gives the European Food Safety Authority's amount for 'Healthy adults in the general population' and leaves out the source's own 'except pregnant women'. Not let out; written again.

read by the editor on 18 November 2026, an hour after it was published (Does kratom have psychoactive effects?): its short answer and its lines are the two reviews' own (stimulant and opioid-like effects; which stands out depends on the amount). Its But is not a limit of that answer: 'Relatively large amounts of kratom need to be consumed before a noticeable psychoactive effect occurs' tells a reader how much it takes to feel the drug. The site gives no such guidance anywhere; no rule caught it because it holds no number (a rule does now: NEEDED_FOR). Taken down; written again by itself.
held.say: Never say how much kratom it takes to feel an effect (no 'large amounts need to be consumed before an effect occurs'). The But must be a limit of the evidence: what kind of work the reviews rest on (one review says that current research is limited to preclinical studies, case reports and surveys). Keep the short answer about which effects kratom has.

held.why: read by the editor on 19 November 2026 (it waited for a further reader that could not be asked): its short answer, its But and its first line rest rightly on FRANK's own words; its line on etizolam says 'A 2022 review' where its source (Wu et al.) is a review of 2023, by its Crossref record. Not let out; written again by itself.
held.say: Give each source the year its reference gives: the review on detecting designer benzodiazepines (Wu et al.) is from 2023, not 2022. Do not repeat the short answer as a line.

held.why: read by the editor on 19 November 2026, after it was published (What is a K-hole?): its short answer and its But rest rightly on the 2024 review ('profound dissociation accompanied by visual and auditory hallucinations'); its first line says the 2025 review finds that a K-hole 'feels like schizophrenia', where the review says its symptoms RESEMBLE those of schizophrenia. Not let out; written again by itself.
held.say: The 2025 review says the K-hole's symptoms resemble those of schizophrenia; it does not say it feels like schizophrenia. Keep the review's own comparison (symptoms that resemble), or leave it out.

held.why: read by the editor on 19 November 2026, after it was published (Are DMT entities a real phenomenon?): it opens with 'Yes.', which a reader takes to mean that the entities exist; its sources say that PERCEIVED encounters with entities are reported and are characteristic of DMT, nothing more. Not let out; written again by itself.
held.say: The sources say that people PERCEIVE encounters with entities, and that such perceived encounters are characteristic of DMT. Do not open with 'Yes', as if the entities themselves had been shown to exist: open with what people report, in the sources' own terms (perceived entity encounters).

held.why: read by the editor on 19 November 2026, after it was published (What is the favourite drug among people?): it answers a question about people in general with one study of 357 low-income adults in treatment in one US region; and 'Younger people preferred opioids; those 40 and older preferred cocaine' contradicts its own source, where alcohol was the most common drug of choice in BOTH age groups and the young were only more likely than the old to name opioids. Its line on synthetic cathinones does not answer the question. Not let out; written again by itself.
held.say: In that study alcohol was the most common drug of choice in BOTH age groups; the younger were only MORE LIKELY than the older to name opioids, the older cocaine: never write 'preferred'. One study of 357 people in treatment cannot say what people in general use most: rest the short answer on an official report or a survey of the general population, or say in its first words who was studied. Leave out lines that do not answer the question.

held.why: read by the editor on 20 November 2026 (held for the editor's reading of answers about amounts): rows 1, 2 and 4 name who received each amount, in trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD, as their sources say; row 3 ('120 mg after the first experimental session', from a sentence of the review's discussion about another study) names nobody ('Participants in an experimental session'), and no row says under what care the amounts were given. Not let out; written again by itself.
held.say: Name who received every amount and under what care, in the source's own terms (people with PTSD in randomized trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy, with therapists present). Leave out an amount whose people the source does not name, such as one taken from a sentence about another study.

held.why: read by the editor on 20 November 2026 (held for the editor's reading of answers about amounts): row 1 is the two trials' own (adult outpatients with treatment-resistant depression, in randomized trials); row 2 ('patients receiving 180 mg of extended-release oral ketamine twice weekly', from the discussion, about another trial) names nobody but 'Patients', and the answer rests on one paper. Not let out; written again by itself.
held.say: Name who received every amount and in what kind of study (adults with treatment-resistant depression in a randomized trial, with the trial's care). Leave out an amount taken from a paper's discussion of another study unless that study's people are named. Rest the answer on more than one source: an official page on esketamine or a review of trials.

held.why: read by the editor on 20 November 2026 (it waited because a reader found it could not be true together with the checked claim cl_can_smoked_cancer): it can be, since the claim says the evidence cannot show either that smoking cannabis raises the risk of lung cancer or that it does not, and the answer's But says the evidence is inconclusive. But its short answer opens with 'It depends.' and never says on what. Not let out; written again by itself.
held.say: Open with what the evidence supports, in the question's terms: it is not proven either way whether smoking cannabis causes cancer. Then what the sources say: cannabis smoke has many of the same cancer-causing chemicals as tobacco smoke (CDC); a 2026 review of studies found a possible link with lung cancer, and says the evidence is inconclusive. Never open with 'It depends' without saying on what.

held.why: read by the editor on 20 November 2026, after it was published (How can ibogaine-related heart attack risk be reduced?): its short answer says the risk 'can be reduced with strict medical observation', where its one source, a review, says ibogaine should be given only by trained medical personnel under strict medical surveillance: a recommendation, not a finding that the risk falls; its second line gives that recommendation in the editor's voice ('Trained medical personnel should monitor the heart'), not the review's. Taken down; written again by itself.
held.say: Say what the review RECOMMENDS as its recommendation ('A 2015 review says ibogaine should be given only by trained medical staff under close heart monitoring'), never that a measure reduces the risk unless a source shows it. Name the risk as the source does (an irregular heartbeat, a long QT interval), and the risk factors it lists.

held.why: read by the editor on 20 November 2026, after it was published (Is PCP associated with violent behavior?): its third line reports a review of 3-methoxy-phencyclidine (3-MeO-PCP), a different drug, as if it were about PCP; and its short answer's second sentence has no subject ('It includes violent behaviors and aggression'). Taken down; written again by itself.
held.say: 3-MeO-PCP is not PCP: leave that review out, or name the drug it is about. Keep to what the sources say of PCP: high doses may cause aggression (Health Canada); violence is often associated with PCP use, and is less common than portrayed (Drug Science). Every sentence with its subject.

held.why: read by the editor on 20 November 2026, after it was published (What is 6-APB like, how does it compare with MDMA, and how risky is it?): it answers 'how risky is it' with 'It can be risky' and a line about MDMA's legal class from an official page on MDMA, which says nothing of 6-APB's risks; 'more entactogenic than MDMA' is given as a fact. Taken down; written again by itself.
held.say: Answer how risky 6-APB is only from what sources say of 6-APB itself (or say that little is known). Do not use a page about MDMA's legal class as a line on risk. Say who reported that 6-APB is more entactogenic than MDMA (people who used it, in surveys or reports), as the review does.

held.why: read by the editor on 20 November 2026, after it was published (What are the effects of kanna?): its short answer says a small study linked kanna to better coping with stress in healthy people, but in that passage the uplifted spirits and the better coping with stress were reported by an earlier study, which the paper cites (the second reader rejected the same claim in a How-do-we-know line); and its first sentence turns a review's line about the plant's reputation into a fact. Taken down; written again by itself.
held.say: Say what each source itself found. The 2014 study (21 healthy people, three weeks, against a placebo) reports ratings of well-being and mood that agreed with an earlier study; the uplifted spirits and the better coping with stress were that earlier study's reports, so say the paper cites them. The 2021 review says the plant has a reputation for calm and well-being: say that, not that kanna does it. Name a limit the sources state.

held.why: read by the editor on 20 November 2026, after it was published (What is 1P-LSD, and how does it compare with LSD?): it never says what 1P-LSD is; its one finding is a sentence of a review of LSD that gives the activity in mice of another compound and says it is close to 1P-LSD's, and the answer reads it as a finding about 1P-LSD ('It compares with LSD in mice studies'); its other line is about clinical research on LSD, not 1P-LSD. Taken down; written again by itself.
held.say: Say what 1P-LSD is only from a source that says it. Read whose activity a sentence gives before saying it of 1P-LSD: in the LSD review the mice result is of another compound, set beside 1P-LSD's. A line about research on LSD itself is not a line about 1P-LSD. If no source here is about 1P-LSD itself, say plainly that little has been studied.

held.why: read by the editor on 20 November 2026, after it was published (What is 5-MeO-DALT like, and how risky is it?): its short answer begins 'It can produce effects like anxiety and nausea' without naming the drug, and gives the powder form as the second half of the answer; its two How-do-we-know lines say only 'dose-dependent effects' and 'a broad range of doses and effects', which tell a reader nothing they can use. Taken down; written again by itself.
held.say: Name the drug in the short answer (5-MeO-DALT, a tryptamine, as the reviews call it). Say which effects and which risks the reviews report, in their measure, and that little has been published, as the But already does. A line that says only 'dose-dependent effects' or 'a broad range of doses and effects' says nothing: say which effects. No line about amounts or doses, and no line about the form it is sold in.
